def: What the body does to a compound over time: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination.
What the compound does to the body: its effect, and how that effect tracks or lags concentration.
Time for blood concentration to fall by half once input stops; an intrinsic property of the molecule.
The plateau where the amount eliminated per interval equals the amount dosed; reached at ~4–5 half-lives.
and trough (min) concentrations within a dosing interval at steady state.
The average concentration across a dosing interval once at steady state.
Volume of blood cleared of compound per unit time; sets how fast it is removed.
The apparent volume the compound spreads into; relates a dose to the plasma concentration it produces.
Fraction of a dose that reaches systemic circulation intact; route-dependent (IV = 100%).
A fixed fraction (not a fixed amount) is cleared per unit time, the basis of the half-life model.
How much a compound builds up with repeat dosing: R = 1 / (1 − ½^(τ/t½)).
Time between doses; its ratio to half-life sets accumulation and peak-to-trough swing.
A larger first dose intended to reach a target exposure sooner. In the simplified bolus model, maintenance × R targets the steady-state post-dose peak; an interval-average target uses 1/(ke × τ).
The standing repeat dose that holds the plateau once it is reached.
Brief, spaced exposures that mimic the body’s natural rhythms (e.g. GH secretagogues).
A flat, sustained level: smooth, but without the natural peaks and troughs the body may expect.
Diminishing response as receptors downregulate under sustained stimulation, the rationale for cycling.
When a long interval lets the level fall below the effective range before the next dose arrives.
Injection into the fat layer under the skin; the common peptide route, moderate-to-high F, slower absorption.
Injection into muscle; faster absorption than subcutaneous.
Absorbed across the nasal mucosa; convenient but variable, usually low bioavailability.
Swallowed; most peptides are degraded in the gut, giving very low bioavailability without protection.
Applied to the skin; local effect with minimal systemic absorption for most peptides.
Dissolving a lyophilized (freeze-dried) peptide in bacteriostatic water before use.
A lab document reporting a batch’s identity, purity, and contaminant test results.
Chromatography: measures purity (the % that is the stated peptide).
Mass spectrometry: confirms identity by measuring the molecule’s mass.
Spectrophotometry used for quantitation / concentration checks.
Bacterial breakdown products that cause reactions if injected; screened by the LAL assay.
Trace metal contaminants screened to safe limits.
A test confirming a batch is free of viable microorganisms.
Combining two or more peptides in one solution; feasibility depends on pH window, vulnerable residues, and reactive additives.
A thymosin beta-4 active-region heptapeptide fragment identified by FDA as TB-500 in its compounding safety-risk page. It is not the same as full-length 43-amino-acid thymosin beta-4/Tβ4.
An albumin-binding moiety that extends half-life from minutes to days (e.g. CJC-1295 DAC).
Attaching a fatty-acid chain so the compound binds albumin and clears slowly (e.g. semaglutide).
Attaching polyethylene-glycol chains to enlarge the molecule and slow clearance.
Fusing to an antibody fragment for a long, antibody-like half-life.
1 mcg = 0.001 mg = one-millionth of a gram.
A potency-based unit; the milligram equivalent is specific to each substance.
Units of liquid volume: 1 mL = 1 cc = one-thousandth of a liter.
On a U-100 syringe, 100 units = 1 mL; these measure volume, not peptide mass.
A molecule that binds a receptor and switches it on, triggering the cell’s response.
A molecule that binds a receptor and blocks it, preventing the normal response.
A compound that prompts a gland or cell to secrete something; a GH secretagogue triggers growth-hormone release.
When cells cut receptor numbers or sensitivity after sustained stimulation, blunting the response over time.
Reading a gene to make RNA, the first step in building a protein; how steroids drive protein synthesis.
Programmed, orderly cell death.
Formation of new blood vessels, part of tissue healing.
Anabolic builds tissue up (muscle, protein); catabolic breaks it down.
Produced naturally within the body, as opposed to taken from outside.
An enzyme that splits peptides into fragments; the main way peptides are cleared.
Freeze-dried into a stable powder; most peptides ship lyophilized and are reconstituted before use.
How tightly a molecule binds its receptor, how readily the key seats in the lock. High affinity means binding even at low concentrations.
How strongly a bound molecule activates the receptor, how hard it turns the key. A molecule can bind tightly yet barely activate.
Binds and activates a receptor but only to a submaximal ceiling, whatever the dose; against a strong natural agonist it can even lower the net signal.
The fast, reversible mute: within minutes, sustained agonist tags a receptor and arrestin uncouples it from its internal relay.
Recovery of responsiveness once stimulation stops, receptors recycle to the surface and synthesis resumes. The gap, not a new drug, restores response.
A protein that clamps onto an activated receptor and disconnects it from its signaling relay, producing rapid desensitization.
When a pathway’s own output signals back to reduce its production, holding the system near a setpoint, like a thermostat.
When a combination produces more than the sum of its parts, one peptide changes conditions so the other works better. True synergy.
Two peptides hitting one goal through different, non-overlapping mechanisms, breadth rather than amplification.
Tβ4 A naturally occurring 43-amino-acid actin-sequestering peptide. It contains methionine and has evidence boundaries, PK, and oxidation assumptions that differ from TB-500/LKKTETQ.
The growth-hormone to insulin-like-growth-factor-1 pathway that many peptides act on.
Shutdown of the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis, the body’s own testosterone production; a key steroid risk.
A gut hormone that lowers blood sugar and appetite; the target of semaglutide and tirzepatide.
The receptor anabolic steroids bind to produce their effects.
A receptor system affecting pigmentation, appetite, and libido; the Melanotan target.
Brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein that supports neuron growth and plasticity.
A signaling molecule that relaxes blood vessels (vasodilation).
A coenzyme central to cellular energy and repair metabolism.
A hormone chain of command from the hypothalamus through the pituitary to a target gland, regulated by feedback from the final hormone.
Hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (LH & FSH) → gonads (testosterone, estrogen): the reproductive axis.
Hypothalamus (CRH) → pituitary (ACTH) → adrenals (cortisol): the stress axis, on a strong daily rhythm.
Growth-hormone-releasing hormone, the hypothalamic “go” signal for GH release, opposed by somatostatin.
The hypothalamic “stop” signal that restrains GH release; its interplay with GHRH makes GH come out in bursts.
LH & FSH. Pulsatile delivery sustains the reproductive axis; continuous delivery suppresses it.
Luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormones, the pituitary gonadotropins that act on the gonads.
The stress-axis releasers: hypothalamic CRH prompts pituitary ACTH, which tells the adrenals to make cortisol.
The adrenal stress hormone; peaks in the early morning and can blunt the reproductive axis.
Insulin-like growth factor 1, made mainly by the liver under GH; carries out most of GH’s growth effects and feeds back to limit GH.
The pituitary cell that makes and releases growth hormone; the shared target of GHRH analogs and GHRPs.
The growth-hormone-secretagogue receptor that GHRPs and ghrelin mimetics bind to trigger GH release.
Aimed at supporting cognition, focus, or memory.
Reducing anxiety.
Acting to clear senescent (worn-out) cells.
A synthetic mimic of a natural growth factor, e.g. IGF-1 LR3.
